wafer-scale-routing.description: A wafer-scale processor uses a connected area much larger than a conventional reticle-sized logic die. Cerebras WSE-3 provides a public example with many compute elements and distributed on-chip SRAM, integrated into a purpose-built system. The attraction is fine-grained local communication and a large aggregate memory fabric. It also demands mechanisms for defect tolerance, routing around unavailable resources, power delivery and heat removal. Wafer-scale integration still has finite storage, routing capacity and fault-tolerance resources; a larger connected surface does not provide unlimited memory. Large models may still need external state movement or system-level streaming, so aggregate local SRAM bandwidth cannot be substituted for external memory bandwidth.

memory-wall-trends.description: The memory wall is a mismatch between useful computation and the ability to store or move its operands. A 2024 paper by Gholami and colleagues reports historical fitted trends for peak compute, DRAM bandwidth and single-GPU capacity. Its Figure 1 and Figure 2 use different samples and normalization, so their trends cannot be combined as though they measured the same population on the same basis. Such fits motivate investigating memory constraints but do not predict a particular future chip or prove that every AI kernel is memory-bound. A workload diagnosis instead measures operation count, transferred bytes, resident state and dependent-access latency at a clearly chosen boundary.

pcie-cxl-semantics.description: PCI Express provides a widely used physical and protocol foundation for host devices. CXL builds on a PCIe physical foundation while adding defined cache and memory semantics alongside I/O. This enables supported devices to participate in coherent access or expose memory through specific host/device roles. It does not make distant memory equivalent to local DRAM: requests still cross links, queues and controllers. Software, firmware and device generation determine what is actually enabled. Both the physical route and the ownership or coherence behavior matter: equal link rates do not imply identical programming semantics.

rack-reference-anatomy.description: A rack-scale accelerator system contains more than GPUs. Compute trays hold CPUs, accelerators, local memory and peripheral devices; switches connect an acceleration domain; management controllers support configuration and recovery. Power shelves and busbars distribute electricity, while manifolds deliver coolant to selected components. NVIDIA’s DGX GB rack guide supplies a concrete NVL72 reference with distinct compute and switch trays. The reference is useful because its interfaces are documented, not because every AI installation uses this design. A tray remains the same assembly when considered through its network, electrical and thermal connections, but each view describes a different service and constraint.

rack-power-conversion.description: Facility electricity reaches a rack through distribution equipment and power supplies, then travels through busbars, board connections and local voltage regulators. Each stage has a voltage, current, capacity and conversion efficiency. The DGX GB reference describes power shelves converting AC to nominal rack DC, but other racks use different arrangements. Nameplate capacity includes redundancy and does not equal measured consumption. At the chip, low voltage implies high current for a given power, increasing the importance of short, low-resistance paths. A power value needs a measurement location before it can constrain compute capacity: input conversion losses and downstream IT demand belong to different boundaries.

production-ramp-allocation.description: A capacity announcement describes a plan or installed capability, while output ramps as equipment, process performance and qualification mature. Inventory can buffer delays, but repeated visits and queued work make factory cycle time longer than processing time. A finished product may then be reserved, contracted or allocated to a different customer. TSMC’s annual report describes customer-linked capacity planning without revealing private allocation shares. Physical output and access require separate accounting: completed equipment can exist without being allocated to the workload in question. Increasing a nominal monthly capacity input must not instantly create finished inventory before its lead time and qualification gates have elapsed.

capacity-phase-geography.description: A cloud region, campus, building, availability zone and project phase are different entities. One campus can operate an early phase while constructing another and announcing a third. Different organizations may describe the same physical capacity as owner, operator, cloud provider or customer, creating double-counting risk. The Stargate and India hub announcements illustrate why dated status belongs to a specific phase and amount. Source date, checked date and power boundary distinguish the reported snapshot from later events; announced megawatts do not automatically count as operating capacity. Counts of factories or access centers require their own definitions and cannot be treated as equal-sized facilities.

regional-siting-access.description: Data-center siting combines electricity readiness, fiber routes, latency, climate, water, staffing and the needs of its users. A project can improve connectivity or electrical infrastructure while remaining under construction. Google’s India hub announcement explicitly links the site with surrounding infrastructure work, while EuroHPC’s gigafactory call describes a public access and procurement mechanism. These are different evidence categories from private installed hardware. Owner, operator and access model are separate attributes. Announced investment does not equal completed equipment, and nearby compute is not automatically available to every local user.

orbital-lifecycle-economics.description: An orbital computing proposal must pay for spacecraft, payloads, launch, ground infrastructure, operations, replacements and lost work. Solar energy availability can change operating inputs but does not erase those costs. Suncatcher’s launch-price analysis is explicitly conditional and incomplete as a total economic study; its projected future launch input must not be presented as a current quote. A fair terrestrial comparison uses the same accepted workload, quality and service targets. Space-generated data reduction and ground-user interactive services can produce very different communication costs. A useful scenario identifies the assumptions that allow its budget to close and any unresolved constraint that prevents a useful service.
